title: Human Physiological Benefits of Viewing Nature: EEG Responses to Exact and Statistical Fractal Patterns
research_question: Do human physiological responses (specifically EEG alpha activity) differ when viewing exact versus statistical fractal patterns, and across different fractal dimensions, to understand if benefits are driven by fractal geometry in general or the specific form found in nature?

participants.description: 35 subjects (17 males, 18 females) in good health, right-handed, with ages ranging from 20 to 66 years (M = 46.2, Md = 49, SD = 14.6).
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but subjects were interviewed for health and handedness before participation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Nine visual stimuli based on the Koch curve, combining three levels of randomness (P: 0.00, 0.25, 0.50) and three fractal dimensions (D: 1.1, 1.3, 1.5). P=0.00 represents exact fractals, while P=0.25 and P=0.50 represent statistical fractals with increasing randomness. Stimuli were shown on a 19-inch LCD screen (37x29.5 cm) for 60 seconds each, separated by a 30-second neutral grey image.

measures.instrument: Quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG) using a Nervus Digital EEG Recorder. Electrodes placed at F3, F4 (frontal), P3, P4 (parietal), T5, T6 (temporal). Alpha frequency band: 9 – 12 Hz.

findings.consequent: Alpha activity in frontal brain areas (F3F4)
findings.mechanism: The natural form of the fractal (statistical, with randomness) is important for inducing alpha responses, indicating a wakefully relaxed state and internalized attention.
findings.quote: alpha increased with P in F3F4 (F(2,66) = 3.82, p < .05)

findings.consequent: Alpha activity in parietal brain areas (P3P4)
findings.quote: alpha increased with P in P3P4 (F(2,66) = 3.26, p < .05)

findings.consequent: Alpha activity in temporal brain areas (T5T6)
findings.quote: alpha increased with P in T5T6 (F(2,68) = 3.53, p < .05)

findings.consequent: Alpha activity in frontal brain areas (F3F4)
findings.mechanism: D values in the region of 1.3-1.5 are perceived to be the most natural and have higher appeal, potentially leading to increased alpha activity.
findings.quote: the effect of D on alpha was significant for F3F4 (F(2,66) = 3.40, p < .05).

findings.consequent: Alpha activity in parietal brain areas (P3P4)
findings.quote: the effect of D on alpha was significant (main effect of D on alpha at P3P4, F(2,66) = 4.19, p < .05)

findings.consequent: Alpha activity in temporal brain areas (T5T6)
findings.quote: the effect of D on alpha was significant (main effect of D on alpha at T5T6, F(2,68) = 3.21, p < .05).

findings.antecedent: Interaction between Randomness (P) and Fractal Dimension (D)
findings.consequent: Alpha activity in parietal brain areas (P3P4)
findings.quote: The interaction effect was significant at P3P4 (linear F(1, 34) = 3.11, p < .05)

findings.antecedent: Interaction between Randomness (P) and Fractal Dimension (D)
findings.consequent: Alpha activity in temporal brain areas (T5T6)
findings.quote: and marginally significant at T5T6 (linear F(1, 33) = 3.79, p < .10).

findings.antecedent: Interaction between Fractal Dimension (D) and hemisphere (left vs. right frontal)
findings.consequent: Alpha activity in frontal brain areas
findings.mechanism: Greater frontal alpha power in the left hemisphere is connected to withdrawal motivation, a tendency to move attention away from stimuli.
findings.quote: a marginally significant interaction effect of D and hemisphere frontally (linear linear F(1,33) = 3.08 p < .10).

findings.mechanism: The randomness adds variation to the repeating pattern, which is important for perception, preference, and holding attention effortlessly.
findings.quote: alpha response was found to be largest for fractals found in nature, i.e. statistical fractals (incorporating high randomness)

findings.antecedent: Fractal dimension D in the region of 1.3-1.5
findings.mechanism: Fractals with D ~ 1.3-1.5 are perceived as most natural and have higher appeal, contributing to a wakefully relaxed state.
findings.quote: and mid to low fractal dimension.

findings.antecedent: Degree of randomness (P) vs. Fractal Dimension (D=1.3)
findings.quote: Concerning the frontal area, alpha increased with randomness while the fractal dimension D = 1.3 had the highest alpha although not significant, that might be due to the fact that there were no higher D than 1.5.

findings.consequent: Alpha activity in parietal and temporal areas
findings.mechanism: Randomness and fractal dimension have opposite effects on alpha activity in these areas, with alpha increasing with randomness and decreasing with fractal dimension.
findings.quote: For the parietal and temporal areas both randomness and fractal dimension had a significant effect on alpha. ... alpha increasing with randomness and decreasing with fractal dimension.

findings.antecedent: Interaction between Randomness (P) and Fractal Dimension (D)
findings.consequent: Alpha activity in parietal and temporal areas
findings.quote: Interaction effects between degree of randomness and fractal dimension could be observed for alpha in the temporal and parietal areas.

mechanisms: The natural form of fractals (statistical fractals with mid-range D values) induces alpha responses, indicating a wakefully relaxed state and internalized attention.
Increased alpha activity reflects active inhibition of non-task relevant areas, top-down processes, and internal attentional control.
The mix of variation (randomness) and predictability in visual patterns allows for effortless attention and mind-wandering, crucial for attention restoration.
Greater frontal alpha power in the left hemisphere is linked to withdrawal motivation, a tendency to direct attention inward.
Moderate environmental stimuli (common nature, mid-D fractals) allow for broader attention.
moderators: Hemisphere (left vs. right frontal brain areas)
implementation_implications: Designing environments with statistical fractal patterns, particularly those with fractal dimensions around 1.3-1.5, may promote relaxation and internalized attention.
Future research should explore two-dimensional fractal patterns, as they are expected to elicit even stronger physiological responses.
limitations: Some subjects were excluded from analyses due to EEG signal artifacts (mostly eye movements).
A limited number of electrode positions were included, focusing on generalized cortical arousal rather than direct visual stimulation (e.g., occipital positions were excluded).
The stimuli used were one-dimensional line fractals, and two-dimensional fractals might elicit stronger responses.
The range of fractal dimensions (D) might have been too limited (no D > 1.5) to fully capture the peak or significance of some effects, particularly for frontal alpha activity.
